{{Short description|French mathematician}}
'''Samuel Lattès''' (21 February 1873 ([[Nice]]) – 5 July 1918) was a French [[mathematician]].<ref name="Alexander2013">{{cite book|author=Daniel S. Alexander|title=A History of Complex Dynamics: From Schröder to Fatou and Julia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pjHwCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA54|date=29 June 2013|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-663-09197-4|page=54}}</ref>

From 1892 to 1895 he studied at the [[École normale supérieure (Paris)|École Normale Superieure]]. After this he was a teacher in [[Algiers]], [[Dijon]] and Nice. After a promotion to [[Paris]] in 1906 he moved first to [[Montpellier]] in 1908 and then to [[Besançon]], before he took up a professorship at the [[University of Toulouse]] in 1911. 

In 1910, he married physicist [[Jeanne Ferrier]], a former student of his, and they had a daughter together.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jeanne Ferrier, épouse Lattès puis Fournier {{!}} PoolCorpus |url=https://poolcorpus.univ-jfc.fr/node/14750 |access-date=2026-09-04 |website=poolcorpus.univ-jfc.fr}}</ref>

He died of [[typhus]] in 1918.

Today Lattès is best known for his work on complex sets, particularly for examples of rational functions including the [[Riemann sphere]] in its [[Julia set]]. Today these examples are described as [[Lattès map]]s or Lattès examples.<ref>Für eine moderne Darstellung der Lattèsschen Beispiele und neuere Ergebnisse dazu siehe: [[John Milnor]], ''On Lattès maps''. In ''Dynamics on the Riemann sphere'', European Mathematical
Society, Zürich, 2006, S. 9–43</ref>
